title: Thirteen Minutes
subtitle: The last minutes of Apollo 11's descent, told as a systems story

hook.text: Seven minutes before Apollo 11 landed, its guidance computer flashed an alarm the crew had never seen in training. This is the thirteen minutes between ignition and touchdown, told through the numbers the room was watching.

context.text: On July 20, 1969, the Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle began its final descent to the Moon's surface. Everything from here on is real: the mission clock, the altitude, the fuel remaining, and the words said in the room. Scroll to follow the descent.

beats.label: Approach
beats.body: The descent engine ignites. For the next twelve minutes, the lunar module falls toward the surface under computer control.

beats.label: Course check
beats.body: Armstrong's landmark checks show Eagle is running long — several miles beyond the planned target. The descent is precise. The position is not.

beats.label: Program alarm
beats.body: Neil Armstrong calls out a 1202. The guidance computer is overloaded — and nobody aboard Eagle knows yet whether that is fatal to the landing.

beats.label: The go call
beats.body: A 26-year-old guidance officer in Houston has twenty-seven seconds from the first alarm call to the answer. The computer is restarting critical jobs and leaving lower-priority work behind.

beats.label: Manual control
beats.body: Armstrong selects the manual landing program, flying by eye over West Crater's boulder field while the computer continues controlling the engine's descent rate.

beats.label: Touchdown
beats.body: Engine off. Postflight analysis found about forty-five seconds of hover time remained — more than it felt like in the room, and still close enough to matter.

takeaway.text: The computer didn't fail because it overloaded. It was built to drop what mattered least and keep what mattered most — which is exactly why it landed on the Moon that day, and why 'graceful degradation' still describes good systems design today.

telemetryNote: Mission time and event altitudes are checked against NASA's Apollo 11 records. Approximate firing-time values are marked ≈; they are inferred from the elapsed descent and NASA's postflight 45-second touchdown margin, not direct cockpit readouts.
